meta.description: King said it — but not this way. Documented 25 March 1966: "injustice in health… the most inhuman because it often results in physical death."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health care is the most shocking and inhumane'?
meta.ogDescription: Chicago, 25 March 1966. The AP-reported wording was "injustice in health", not "health care", and "inhuman", not "inhumane".

answer.label: Martin Luther King Jr. — but not in these words
answer.authorDates: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister and civil rights leader
answer.sourceLine: King really did say this, on 25 March 1966, to reporters in Chicago before he addressed the second convention of the Medical Committee for Human Rights. The wording that circulates today is not the wording anyone recorded: the Associated Press account published the next day reads “Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman because it often results in physical death” — health, not health care; inhuman, not inhumane; and with a final clause the famous version drops. No transcript or recording of the speech itself has ever been located.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed wording, genuine speaker — the thought is King’s, the sentence is a later smoothing.

source.heading: What King is documented as saying

docMeta.dd: Press conference before King’s address to the second convention of the Medical Committee for Human Rights, Chicago
“injustice in health… the most inhuman” — not “health care… inhumane”

source.excerpt: We are concerned about the constant use of federal funds to support this most notorious expression of segregation. Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman because it often results in physical death.
trail: 25 March 1966 — King speaks to reporters in Chicago before addressing the Medical Committee for Human Rights; he and MCHR officers accuse the American Medical Association of a “conspiracy of inaction” on civil rights (Physicians for a National Health Program ↗).

26 March 1966 — the Associated Press wire report gives the earliest published version: “Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman because it often results in physical death” (Quote Investigator ↗).

29 March 1966 — the Woodlawn Booster prints a different rendering — “Of all forms of discrimination and inequalities, injustice in health is the most shocking and inhuman” — possibly taken from the convention speech rather than the press conference (Quote Investigator ↗).

18 January 2013 — Amanda Moore reports that the King Center, Stanford’s King research institute and other archives could produce no text, transcript or recording — but Dr. Quentin Young, who chaired the Medical Committee for Human Rights, confirmed he heard King say it, and that the word was “inhuman” (HuffPost ↗).
source.excerptNote: The fuller passage as set out in Charlene Galarneau’s study of the quotation, drawn from press accounts of the 25 March 1966 press conference. King’s complete remarks were never transcribed or recorded, so this is the best-documented rendering rather than a verbatim text.

source.rightsHolder: Estate of Martin Luther King, Jr., Inc. (King’s spoken remarks); the Associated Press (the 1966 wire report)
source.rightsNote: King spoke these words in 1966 and they first reached print in an Associated Press wire report of 26 March 1966 — far too recent for the public domain in the United States, where his words are administered by the King estate and the wire text belongs to the Associated Press. The reworded “health care… inhumane” sentence has no identified author at all, so nothing about it can be claimed as free to use.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.metaLine: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister, civil rights leader, Nobel Peace Prize 1964
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and the most prominent leader of the civil rights movement, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. By 1966 he was living and organising in Chicago, and his campaigning had widened from voting rights and desegregation to housing, poverty and — at the Medical Committee for Human Rights that March — segregated hospitals and the death rates that followed from them. He is one of the most heavily misquoted figures in English, which is why his genuine lines deserve their genuine wording.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in an Associated Press report of King’s press conference in Chicago, published 26 March 1966: “Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman because it often results in physical death.” A differing rendering appeared in the Woodlawn Booster, 29 March 1966. See Charlene Galarneau, “Getting King’s Words Right,” Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved 29, no. 1 (2018): 5–8. No transcript or recording of the speech is known.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health care is the most shocking and inhumane’?” Last verified 4 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: Reworded. Martin Luther King Jr. made this remark at a Chicago press conference on March 25, 1966, before addressing the Medical Committee for Human Rights — but the documented wording, from the Associated Press report of March 26, 1966, is "Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman because it often results in physical death." No transcript or recording of the speech is known. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: A real statement, quietly rewritten
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication pinned on a famous name. It is something rarer and easier to miss: a genuine King statement that has been edited in transmission, word by word, until the version everyone shares differs from every version anyone recorded.

items.why: Every 1966 account says “injustice in health.” The swap to “health care” narrows King’s point from health itself — and the conditions that shape it — to the delivery of medical services (Physicians for a National Health Program ↗).
The reported word is “inhuman.” Dr. Quentin Young, who chaired the Medical Committee for Human Rights and heard King speak, insisted on that word and thought it the stronger of the two (HuffPost ↗).

The Associated Press account ends “…because it often results in physical death.” That clause — the whole reason King called this inequality the most shocking one — is absent from the sentence usually quoted (Quote Investigator ↗).

The reworded line is printed by serious organisations with nothing more than “a 1966 speech to the Medical Committee for Human Rights” behind it — as on the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation’s blog ↗ — so each repetition looks sourced without ever adding a source.

misattribution.truthLine: Best available verdict: King said it, on 25 March 1966 in Chicago, but the documented words are “Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman because it often results in physical death” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why King was talking to doctors
lead: The Medical Committee for Human Rights was founded in June 1964 by health professionals who went to Mississippi to treat civil rights workers and volunteers during Freedom Summer. By its second convention, in Chicago in March 1966, the group had turned from field medicine to the structure of American medicine itself — segregated hospitals, and the federal money that kept them running. King and MCHR officers used the occasion to accuse the American Medical Association of a “conspiracy of inaction” on civil rights.

That is the sentence’s real setting, and it explains what the rewriting costs. King was not making a general appeal for medical coverage; he was saying that segregation in health kills people, which is why he called it the most shocking inequality of all. Strip the closing clause and swap “health” for “health care” and you get a gentler, more quotable line that means something narrower than what he said.
detailsBody: Amanda Moore went looking for the source in January 2013 and found a closed loop: everyone citing everyone, no one citing King. The King Center in Atlanta, Stanford’s King research institute and university rare-book collections could not produce a text, transcript or recording of the 1966 address. What broke the loop was testimony, not paper — Dr. Quentin Young, present as an MCHR leader, confirming he heard it said, and correcting “inhumane” back to “inhuman” (HuffPost ↗).

Charlene Galarneau, who teaches in Harvard Medical School’s master of bioethics programme, later set out the documentary case in “Getting King’s Words Right” in the Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, volume 29, issue 1 (2018), pages 5–8 — the reference health-equity writers now cite when they use the line carefully (Harvard Center for Bioethics ↗).
